claim.pdf_says: 15.69.4   Returned values rules  (printed in the same bold subclause style and at the same outline depth as 15.69.1 General, 15.69.2 General format, 15.69.3 Argument rules on the preceding page)
claim.why_it_matters: The heading is emitted at level 2 while every sibling subclause of 15.69 is level 3 (`### 15.69.1 General`, `### 15.69.2 General format`, `### 15.69.3 Argument rules`) and every analogous subclause elsewhere in this batch is level 3 (`### 15.70.4`, `### 15.71.4`, `### 15.72.4`). At `##` it becomes a sibling of `## 15.69 NUMVAL-F function` rather than its child, so the returned-value rules detach from the NUMVAL-F function clause in any TOC or outline walk. The break coincides exactly with the page-928/929 boundary, which is where the level was lost.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED on four independent grounds; the two source quotes are accurate but the finding is a formatting artifact, not a content discrepancy. (1) NOTHING IS MISSING. The kind 'missing-heading' is a misnomer. specs/ISO_COBOL.md:37189 carries the heading verbatim - correct clause number, correct title ('Returned values rules', plural 'values', matching the printed page), and the correct anchor ``. All three normative rules on the page are transcribed completely and accurately (rule 1 spaces-ignored; rule 2 native/standard-binary approximation; rule 3 standard-decimal exact). No spec text is lost, altered, or reflowed away. (2) THE PDF HAS NO ##/### DISTINCTION TO LOSE. I cropped and inspected the printed glyphs at 300 dpi. On p928 the PARENT clause '15.69 NUMVAL-F function' and the CHILD subclause '15.69.1 General' are set in the identical bold face, at the identical point size, flush at the identical left margin - the typography draws no distinction whatsoever between a two-part clause number and a three-part subclause number. '15.69.4 Returned values rules' on p929 is that same face and size; its small right-shift versus p928 is the mirrored odd/even page margin, confirmed because the body line '1) Leading, trailing, and embedded spaces are ignored.' carries exactly the same offset. The document's only depth cue is the dotted number itself, which the transcription reproduces exactly. So the claim's premise - 'printed ... at the same outline depth as 15.69.1' - is true but vacuous: 15.69 is printed at that same depth too, and one cannot derive a required markdown heading level from this PDF. (3) THE CLAIMED HARM IS FALSE AS STATED. Every page block in the transcription opens with `## Page NNN` followed by `# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)` - 941 such H1 running headers across the file. That H1 resets the outline to depth 1 at the top of page 929. Consequently page 929's first clause heading cannot nest under `## 15.69 NUMVAL-F function` (page 928) whether it is written `##` or `###`; changing it to `###` would reparent it under page 929's running header, not under the NUMVAL-F clause. The detachment the claimant describes is produced by per-page running-header furniture and is entirely unaffected by the proposed fix. (4) NOT PAGE-SPECIFIC, AND THE PAGE-BREAK CORRELATION DOES NOT HOLD. `## ..` occurs 274 times in specs/ISO_COBOL.md against 1256 `### ..` occurrences - roughly 18% of all three-part headings, a document-wide markup convention inconsistency present from clause 4.2.5 onward, not a page-929 defect. Scanning every page block, 359 pages whose first three-part heading is `##` versus 70 whose first is `###`, so 'the break coincides exactly with the page-928/929 boundary, which is where the level was lost' does not single out this page or this boundary. Rejected under the stated criteria: the text is present, the difference is markup formatting plus page furniture, and no meaning changes. A global heading-level normalization pass over the transcription may be worth doing on its own merits, but it is not a PDF-versus-markdown content discrepancy and does not belong in a per-page reconciliation ledger.
